title: How Habits Take Hold
titleJa: 習慣はどのように身につくのか：習慣形成の心理学

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Think back over the first hour of your day. You probably woke up, reached for your phone, washed, dressed and ate breakfast in much the same order as you did yesterday, and with very little conscious thought. Psychologists estimate that a large share of everyday behaviour consists of actions repeated in the same place and at roughly the same time each day. What defines habits, however, is that they are triggered automatically by the situation we are in, rather than by a deliberate decision. This automatic quality is extremely useful: because familiar tasks can run on their own, the mind is free to concentrate on other matters.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Many researchers describe habits in terms of a simple loop with three parts. First comes a cue: a time of day, a location, a particular emotion or the action that has just been completed. The cue prompts a routine, which is the behaviour itself. Finally there is a reward – a pleasant feeling, a sense of relief or simply the satisfaction of having finished something – which makes the brain more likely to repeat the routine the next time the cue appears. With enough repetition, the connection between cue and routine becomes so strong that the reward is no longer needed. In laboratory studies, animals that have been trained for long enough continue to perform a learned action even after the reward has been taken away.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How long, then, does it take for a new habit to form? A widely repeated answer is twenty-one days. The figure appears in countless books and websites, yet its origins are unclear; it seems to have come from self-help writing of the mid-twentieth century rather than from any scientific study. Researchers have long suspected that the real answer is less tidy.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: To investigate the question, Dr Miriam Okafor and her colleagues at a Canadian university followed 140 adult volunteers for twelve weeks. Each participant chose one new behaviour and attached it to an event that already happened every day: drinking a glass of water after breakfast, for example, or going for a ten-minute walk after lunch. Every evening, participants completed a short online questionnaire on which they rated how automatic the behaviour had felt that day. For most people, the scores rose quickly during the first few weeks and then climbed more and more slowly, as if approaching a ceiling. On average, this ceiling was reached after about ten weeks, but the variation between individuals was considerable. Simple actions such as drinking water became automatic in as little as three weeks, whereas several participants who were trying to exercise regularly had still not reached the ceiling when the study ended.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Research of this kind also casts doubt on a familiar assumption: that changing behaviour is mainly a matter of willpower. The Swedish psychologist Dr Lars Hedlund asked several hundred people to record, at random moments during the day, whether they were currently trying to resist a temptation. Surprisingly, those who scored highest on a standard test of self-control reported resisting temptation less often than the others, not more. Hedlund's explanation is that such people seldom need to fight their impulses at all. Instead, they arrange their lives so that temptation rarely arises, relying on well-established routines rather than on constant effort. This suggests that willpower is overrated.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If good habits are hard to build, bad ones are hard to break, because the link between cue and routine does not simply disappear when we decide to stop. The most effective strategies therefore work on the cue rather than on the routine. Someone who wants to snack less, for instance, might stop buying biscuits instead of relying on resisting them every evening. Researchers have also noticed that major life changes, such as moving house or starting a new job, offer a valuable opportunity, since the familiar cues that once triggered old habits are suddenly absent.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These ideas are beginning to influence public health campaigns. Traditional campaigns have tended to focus on information, warning people of the risks of smoking or inactivity. Knowledge matters, but on its own it rarely changes behaviour that is repeated daily. Newer programmes try to build cues directly into people's surroundings. In one primary school programme, for example, bright stickers were placed above every sink in the school, and children washed their hands at fixed times, immediately before lunch and after break. Within a term, teachers reported that most pupils were washing their hands without being reminded. Health planners are also learning to target people at moments of transition, such as the birth of a first child or retirement, when existing routines are already being disrupted.

groups.instructions: Questions 1–6. Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage? Write TRUE if the statement agrees with the information, FALSE if the statement contradicts the information, NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this.

questions.text: Once an action has become a habit, the mind can focus on other things while it is being performed.
questions.explanation: A段落に "because familiar tasks can run on their own, the mind is free to concentrate on other matters" とあります。慣れた作業が自動で進むので心は他のことに集中できる、という内容と一致するので TRUE です。

questions.text: A well-established habit stops as soon as its reward is removed.
questions.explanation: B段落に "the connection between cue and routine becomes so strong that the reward is no longer needed" とあり、動物も "even after the reward has been taken away" 行動を続けると書かれています。報酬がなくなっても習慣は続くので、設問文と矛盾し FALSE です。

questions.text: It is not certain where the idea of a twenty-one-day period for forming habits comes from.
questions.explanation: C段落に "The figure appears in countless books and websites, yet its origins are unclear" とあります。its origins are unclear が「どこから来たのか確かではない」の言い換えなので TRUE です。

questions.text: In Okafor's study, older volunteers needed more time to form a habit than younger ones.
questions.explanation: D段落には "140 adult volunteers" とあるだけで、参加者の年齢による違いには触れていません。本文で比べられているのは "Simple actions such as drinking water" と運動という行動の種類の違いなので、NOT GIVEN です。

questions.text: People with high scores for self-control reported resisting temptation more often than other people.
questions.explanation: E段落に "those who scored highest on a standard test of self-control reported resisting temptation less often than the others, not more" とあります。自制心の高い人ほど誘惑に抵抗した回数は「少なかった」ので、設問文と矛盾し FALSE です。

questions.text: Health campaigns based on information are more expensive than those that change people's surroundings.
questions.explanation: G段落は情報中心の従来型キャンペーンについて "on its own it rarely changes behaviour that is repeated daily" と効果の限界を述べていますが、費用の比較はどこにもありません。効果の話を費用の話と取り違えないことが大切で、NOT GIVEN です。

groups.instructions: Questions 7–10. Complete the summary using the list of words, A–J, below.

questions.text: Each volunteer linked a new behaviour to an existing daily ____.
questions.explanation: D段落の "attached it to an event that already happened every day" が根拠で、毎日すでに起きている出来事（朝食・昼食など）を activity と言い換えています。A の reward は B段落で説明される習慣のループの3番目の要素で、新しい行動を結びつけた対象ではありません。

questions.text: Every evening, they rated how ____ the behaviour had felt that day.
questions.explanation: D段落に "they rated how automatic the behaviour had felt that day" とあります。評価したのは行動の「自動性」であり、楽しさ（D pleasant）や難しさ（I difficult）ではありません。

questions.text: For most people, progress was ____ during the first few weeks but slowed down later.
questions.explanation: D段落に "the scores rose quickly during the first few weeks and then climbed more and more slowly" とあり、最初の数週間は伸びが速かったので rapid が入ります。B の steady は「一定のペースで」の意味になり、途中で伸びが鈍った本文の内容に合いません。

questions.text: Simple actions became automatic within a few weeks, but some people trying to take regular ____ had still not reached the ceiling after twelve weeks.
questions.explanation: D段落に "several participants who were trying to exercise regularly had still not reached the ceiling when the study ended" とあります。take regular exercise が try to exercise regularly の言い換えです。H の rest（休息）は本文に出てきません。

groups.instructions: Questions 11–13. Answer the questions below. Choose NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.

questions.text: According to Hedlund, what do people with strong self-control depend on instead of constant effort?
questions.explanation: E段落の "relying on well-established routines rather than on constant effort" が根拠です。depend on が relying on、instead of が rather than の言い換えになっています。willpower は筆者が過大評価されていると述べているものなので答えになりません。

questions.text: What kind of events give people a valuable opportunity to change their habits?
questions.explanation: F段落に "major life changes, such as moving house or starting a new job, offer a valuable opportunity" とあります。moving house や starting a new job は具体例なので、まとめた表現である major life changes を答えます。

questions.text: In the school programme, where were the stickers placed?
questions.explanation: G段落に "bright stickers were placed above every sink in the school" とあります。above every sink in the school では3語を超えるので、above every sink と書きます。

vocab.ja: （反応などを）引き起こす、きっかけとなる
（答えなどが）すっきりした、単純な
